doc.title: Fred Wesley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 21, 2024

title: Writing out horn parts on the bus for James Brown sessions
summary: Writing parts was tedious; he did it on the bus without instruments, learning by doing, and eventually found score pads.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well you set up one of my questions that I’ve really been curious about so we can jump there. I used to be — I’ve been in a lot of bands and as a horn player for some reason I got the job of writing out the horn parts that we were hearing on records. And it was a laborious process, especially with those funk rhythms and all the sixteenth rests. When you talked about not doing that until you were with James Brown, was it tedious for you to write those parts out or didn’t you even write them out?
It was very tedious. And I did write some of them out. Some of them I just gave to the guys you know, for them to play. What instrument do you play?

Saxophone. Well I gave a saxophone player this part, trombone, the trumpet player their part. But I had to write out the music when I had to use the New York studio musicians on the session. And I really didn’t know how to do it and I had to write them out as we rode on the bus. So I didn’t have a piano, I didn’t have a trombone, I couldn’t play the trombone, I had to — it was a tedious, tedious process you know. And like you said, a tedious process that I had to do and I had to find out what note was — find one note and then find another note from that one note that I knew you know. And it was a very tedious process. But it worked out real good for me because now I knew how to do that kind of automatically you know, without knowing what I’m doing. You know?
There is something about that statement it’s just so wonderful. Like you know what you’re doing but you don’t know what you’re doing.
I guess you mean that from a theoretical standpoint, that students learn now in jazz school and so forth. But is it harder to write for two horns or five?

Well definitely it’s harder to write for five horns, you know, because you have to hear all the notes in the chords and the movements of the different instruments you know. And you have to — like alto — I’ve never learned how to write for alto really good you know, because it was in between and the B flat horns and the C horns. You know? And you have to hear that kind of stuff and write it down. It was very tedious you know. But I didn’t mind doing it, if it took me all night and all day sometimes so that I’d just sleep for days you know. But I learned by doing you know.
Did you have a score pad on the bus?

Sometimes. Sometimes I did. I eventually got a score pad. But usually I would just write it out. You’d be surprised what I used to write on. Sometimes I’d draw a staff and write on the staff you know. But yeah, I finally got that score pad, when I found out what a score pad was. And I said, oh you can do it? It’s already written out?
